chunks: Hisham ibn al-Hakam said to me:

There was an atheist in Egypt who had heard certain things about Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). So he went out to Medina in order to debate with him, but did not find him there. He was told that the Imam had gone out to Mecca. So he went out to Mecca, and we were with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) during the tawaf. His (the atheist's) name was Abd al-Malik and his kunya was Abu Abdillah.

He struck his own shoulder against the shoulder of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him: 'What is your name?' He said: 'My name is Abd al-Malik.' He asked: 'And what is your kunya?' He said: 'My kunya is Abu Abdillah.' So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Then who is this king whose slave you are? Is he from the kings of the earth or from the kings of the sky? And inform me about your son — is he the slave of the god of the sky or the slave of the god of the earth? Say whatever you like, you will be refuted either way.'

Hisham ibn al-Hakam said: I said to the atheist: 'Are you not going to respond to him?' He (the narrator) said that the atheist found fault with my words. Then Abu Abdillah said: 'When we are done with the tawaf, come to us.' So when Abu Abdillah finished, the atheist came to him and sat in his presence, and we were gathered around him.

So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to the atheist: 'Do you know that the earth has an underneath and an above?' He said: 'Yes.' He asked: 'Have you entered its underneath?' He said: 'No.' He asked: 'Then what would make you know what is beneath it?' He said: 'I don't know, except that I suppose there is nothing beneath it.' So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Conjecture is helplessness regarding that of which you are not certain.'

Then Abu Abdillah said: 'Have you ascended to the sky?' He said: 'No.' He asked: 'Do you know what is in it?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'How strange your case is! You have not reached the east and not reached the west and not descended into the earth and not ascended to the sky, and not passed through there to know what is beyond them — yet you deny what is in them. Would a rational person deny what he does not know?' The atheist said: 'No one has spoken to me like this before you.' So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'So you are in doubt about this — perhaps He exists and perhaps He does not.' The atheist said: 'Perhaps that is so.'

So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'O man! The one who does not know has no argument against the one who knows, and there is no argument for the ignorant. O brother of the people of Egypt, understand what I say, for we never doubt in God, ever! Do you not see the sun and the moon, and the night and the day following their course? They do not get confused and they return, for they are compelled. There is no place for them except their assigned place. So if they had power to go away, why would they return? And if they were not compelled, why would night not become day and day not become night? They are compelled, by God, O brother of the people of Egypt, to their perpetuity. And the One who compelled them is wiser than both of them and greater.' So the atheist said: 'You speak the truth.'

Then Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him) said: O brother of the people of Egypt, that which you adhere to and think to be the eternal time — if time takes them away, why does it not bring them back? And if it brings them back, why does it not take them away? The people are compelled. O brother of the people of Egypt, why is the sky raised up and the earth laid down? Why does not the sky fall upon the earth? Why does not the earth slide down beyond its layers? They do not hold each other, nor do those upon it hold on. The atheist said: Allah, their Lord and Master, holds them both.

He [Hisham] said: So the atheist believed at the hands of Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him). Humran said to him: May I be made your ransom — if the atheists believe at your hand, then the disbelievers believed at the hands of your father. The believer who had believed at the hands of Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him) said: Make me among your students. Abu Abd Allah said: O Hisham ibn al-Hakam, take him to yourself and teach him. So Hisham taught him, and he became the teacher of the people of al-Sham and the people of Egypt in faith, and his purity became so excellent that Abu Abd Allah was pleased with it.

key_terms.اضطرّ: Compelled/forced -- a key theological term indicating that the celestial bodies are compelled by a higher power, proving the existence of a Compelling Creator
key_terms.الدهر: Time/fate -- the pre-Islamic materialist concept that time alone governs existence, which the Imam refutes
key_terms.الظن: Supposition/conjecture -- as opposed to certain knowledge (yaqin), used here to show the weakness of denying God based on mere assumption
key_terms.حجة: Proof/argument -- used in the principle that the ignorant has no argument against the knowledgeable
key_terms.زنديق: Zindiq -- an atheist, heretic, or one who denies the existence of God, derived from Persian, commonly used in early Islamic theological literature

ai.seo_question: How did Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq prove the existence of God to an atheist?
ai.summary: This hadith narrates the famous debate between Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) and an Egyptian atheist (zindiq) that took place during the tawaf in Mecca. The Imam systematically dismantled the atheist's denial of God through a series of rational arguments: he showed that conjecture about the unknown is weakness, that denying what one has never investigated is irrational, and that the orderly alternation of day and night, the suspension of the sky, and the stability of the earth all point to a compelling, wise Creator. The atheist, who had originally come seeking to defeat the Imam in debate, instead embraced faith. The encounter demonstrates the Shia intellectual tradition's emphasis on rational theology (kalam) and the role of the Imams as authoritative defenders of monotheism.
